text: Joseph Melville Broughton Jr. (November 17, 1888 – March 6, 1949) was an American politician who served as the 60th governor of North Carolina from 1941 to 1945 and later briefly as a United States senator from January 3, 1949, until his death in office approximately two months later. Born in Raleigh, North Carolina, he graduated from Wake Forest College in 1910, where he played football, attended Harvard Law School, and worked as a school principal and journalist before entering the legal profession. He served in the North Carolina Senate from 1927 to 1929 and later served one term as governor. Identified with progressive politics, including support for Roosevelt Administration social justice legislation, he implemented several reforms, most notably extending the public school term from six to nine months. The North Carolina Department of Natural and Cultural Resources describes him as a typical white moderate of his time, advocating for African American improvements such as equalizing teacher salaries and improving housing. In August 1941, he deployed the North Carolina National Guard to protect Cy Winstead, a Black man accused of raping a white woman, after he was nearly lynched in Roxboro. Following the incident, Broughton had police investigate the mob and charged ten white men; on April 24, 1942, a jury found five—Coy Harris, A.P. Spriggs, P.I. Holt, Johnny Holt, and Willie Aiken—guilty of unlawful assembly for an unlawful purpose, a misdemeanor punishable by up to two years in prison, while acquitting them of inciting to riot. Harris and Spriggs were each sentenced to 18 months in county jail, and the other three to 12 months. The jury recommended mercy for the Colt brothers, and Aiken did not deny his guilt. The verdict shocked the public, which had been sympathetic to the mob; in June 1942, 2,000 people submitted a petition demanding parole or pardon. Harris, Spriggs, P.L. Holt, and Aiken were paroled on July 23, 1942; Johnny Holt was denied parole due to his involvement in a California robbery and was paroled between then and 1943; all six were discharged from parole in September 1943. Winstead later pleaded guilty to assault with intent to commit rape and was sentenced to two and a half to five years in prison; in February 1943, the Person County NAACP petitioned for his parole, expressing doubt about his guilt, but he refused to apply due to strict conditions. Broughton resisted threats to segregation; in 1942, he urged African Americans not to make demands during World War II, stating, "Negroes are ill-advised if they take the position they are for victory in this war if something is to be done for them. Negroes should put their full energy into the war effort, for failure means slavery of the worst sort for white and Negro alike. The man or woman who uses this emergency as a means of stirring up strife between the races is not a friend to either race and is not a good American." In 1943, he wrote, "We believe in a policy of purity and high standard as to both races and we recognize the principle that race distinction does not imply race discrimination," and rejected NAACP criticism, claiming racism had no impact on North Carolina's judicial system. He was one of twelve nominated at the 1944 Democratic National Convention to serve as Franklin D. Roosevelt's running mate. In 1948, Broughton was elected to the U.S. Senate after defeating William B. Umstead in the Democratic primary; he won both a special election to complete the Senate term and a full-term election in November and took office on December 31, 1948, though his service was brief. Appearing healthy, he suddenly collapsed from a heart attack and died in Washington, D.C., on March 6, 1949. Governor W. Kerr Scott appointed Frank Porter Graham to fill his vacant Senate seat until the next election. Broughton was the son of Joseph Melville Broughton and Sallie Harris; he married Alice Willson in 1916 and had four children. He was the nephew of Needham B. Broughton and a first cousin of Carrie Lougee Broughton and medical doctor and Baptist minister Len G. Broughton. He and his wife lived in the Jolly-Broughton House in Raleigh's Hayes Barton Historic District before and after residing in the North Carolina Executive Mansion. He was interred at Montlawn Memorial Park in Raleigh. In 1959, the State Hospital at Morganton for psychiatric patients was renamed Broughton Hospital in his memory, and Broughton Hall at North Carolina State University was named in his honor. He was a member of Civitan International.
